---
title: "Quiz: training GANs and what goes wrong"
---

Short questions on mode collapse, oscillation, the Wasserstein idea and judging samples. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A GAN trained on cell images produces sharp, realistic cells, but almost all of them are round interphase nuclei; no dividing cells appear. What is this failure called, and which of precision and recall shows it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Realism or variety?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Mode dropping (in the extreme, mode collapse). Precision stays high (the samples are realistic); recall is low (part of the real variety, the dividing cells, has no samples nearby).
:::

---

**Q2.** Why does nothing in the generator's loss reward variety?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The loss is an average over samples of $-\log D(G(z))$. What is best for each sample on its own?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each sample is scored on its own: for a fixed discriminator the best is to put every sample where $D$ is highest. Variety only comes from the discriminator reacting to the pile-up.
:::

---

**Q3.** The data and the generated distribution do not overlap at all. Their Jensen–Shannon divergence is $\ln 2$. What is it after the generator has moved halfway towards the data, still without overlap? What does this mean for training?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
JS depends only on the overlap.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Still $\ln 2$. The divergence does not change, so it gives no slope: the generator gets no signal about which way the data are (vanishing gradients). The earth mover's (Wasserstein) distance has halved, so it does give a slope.
:::

---

**Q4.** Two equally large samples in 1D: $(4, 0, 2)$ and $(1, 5, 3)$. What is their Wasserstein-1 distance?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Sort both, pair by rank.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sorted: $(0, 2, 4)$ and $(1, 3, 5)$; every pair is 1 apart, so $W_1 = 1$.
:::

---

**Q5.** The generator loss of your GAN rises during training. Is training going badly?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Against whom is the loss measured?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not necessarily: a stronger discriminator raises the generator's loss even when the samples get better. Judge by the samples, precision and recall on held-out data, not by the losses.
:::

---

**Q6.** You compute precision and recall of 1 000 generated cell images against 1 000 real ones and get precision 0.97, recall 0.95. Name one problem these numbers cannot rule out.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What if the generator copies its training images?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Memorisation: copies of training images score well on both. Check the distance of each sample to its nearest **training** image (it should not be much smaller than for held-out real images). Also: the metrics live in a feature space, so differences the features ignore (e.g. intensities you want to measure) are invisible.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* With simultaneous gradient steps of size $\eta$ on the game $\min_x\max_y xy$, by what factor does the distance from the equilibrium grow per step?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$x \leftarrow x - \eta y$, $y \leftarrow y + \eta x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(x - \eta y)^2 + (y + \eta x)^2 = (1 + \eta^2)(x^2 + y^2)$: the distance grows by $\sqrt{1 + \eta^2}$ per step, for every $\eta > 0$.
:::
